newsitem.title: INDIA: Banks urge India to launch rupee derivatives.
newsitem.headline: Banks urge India to launch rupee derivatives.

text.p: India's delay in introducing exchange risk products like rupee derivatives could prove costly in the long run, bankers told the country's central bank on Saturday.
"If we don't (introduce derivatives), these markets may move offshore -- already signs are there it is moving," Arvind Sethi, head of India treasury at ANZ Grindlays Bank told a seminar.
Foreign investment in India would become costlier if exchange risks are not hedged within the country, Sethi said. This would compound the inherent problems of an already high-cost economy.
But Reserve Bank of India (RBI) officials said their overtures had not been encouragingly received by Indian banks.

"We took a number of steps in the last two to three months," an RBI official told the seminar, organised by the Forex Association of India. "The response we found, to be candid, was not encouraging," he said.
"This left us wondering whether those who are articulating demands are aware of what the market wants."
The maturity shown by market players -- banks as well as corporates -- would determine the pace of reforms in the foreign exchange market, he said.
Bankers said the RBI official was referring to banks and companies not making use of the cross-currency swaps facility.

Pavan Sukhdev, country treasurer of Deutsche Bank, wondered if banks were actually selling what customers wanted or if they preferred to focus on profitable high-end products such as structured finance.
Bankers said some of India's well-known firms with sizeable foreign exchange exposure were ignorant of hedging products.
An official with one of India's largest petrochemical firms said many bankers were themselves unable to explain derivatives and their implications to firms.
"Corporates should not be expected to offer their exposures to banks on a platter," he said.

Most speakers at the seminar said the lack of a term-money market in India blocked the way to the creation of rupee derivatives. RBI's practice of charging reserve requirements on inter-bank borrowing has contributed to this, they said.

When the market rates underlying derivatives are themselves not transparent, it is difficult to develop derivatives, some bankers said. India does not have a reference rate comparable to LIBOR or KLIBOR.

An official with Citibank said a dollar-rupee Indian options market hedged by the forward dollar market rates could be created, provided the central bank put in place a regulatory mechanism for the option-writing banks.
